evidence: gd.txt

Findings: CryptoCurrency:EC2/BitcoinTool.B,
UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/TorIPCaller.
Need: continuous, no agents.
scenarios.hint: Which service produces these exact finding types?
scenarios.situation: Findings show EC2 crypto-mining and an IAM user calling APIs from a Tor exit node; the team needs continuous agentless detection.
scenarios.title: Reading the findings
scenarios.why: GuardDuty is the threat-detection service producing finding types like CryptoCurrency:EC2/BitcoinTool and UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/TorIPCaller, using ML and threat intel with no agents. Config evaluates configuration; CloudTrail is the log source; Inspector assesses vulnerabilities, not threats.

evidence: insp.txt

Need: scan EC2 AMIs and Lambda
functions for CVEs, continuously,
prioritized by risk.
scenarios.hint: Which service scans for software vulnerabilities rather than active threats?
scenarios.situation: The team needs continuous CVE scanning of EC2 instances, AMIs, and Lambda functions, prioritized by risk.
scenarios.title: Scanning for CVEs
scenarios.why: Inspector continuously scans EC2, ECR images, and Lambda for software vulnerabilities and network exposure, with risk-based prioritization. GuardDuty detects active threats; Security Hub aggregates findings; WAF filters web traffic.

evidence: hub.txt

Findings from GuardDuty, Inspector,
Macie, Config in 4 accounts.
Need: one prioritized view + CIS
benchmark scores.
scenarios.hint: Which service aggregates security findings into a single pane with standards checks?
scenarios.situation: Findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, and Config across 4 accounts need one prioritized view plus CIS benchmark scoring.
scenarios.title: One pane for all findings
scenarios.why: Security Hub aggregates findings from multiple security services across accounts into normalized ASFF findings with automated checks against standards like CIS. The others are finding producers, not aggregators.

evidence: macie.txt

50 TB in S3. Need: find PII/PHI,
flag unencrypted sensitive buckets,
monitor access anomalies.
scenarios.hint: Which service uses ML to discover sensitive data in S3?
scenarios.prompt: Which service discovers the sensitive data?
scenarios.situation: 50 TB in S3 needs automated discovery of PII/PHI, detection of unencrypted sensitive buckets, and access-anomaly monitoring.
scenarios.title: Finding the PII in 50 TB
scenarios.why: Macie uses ML to discover and classify sensitive data (PII, PHI, credentials) in S3 and monitors access patterns. GuardDuty detects threats, Config evaluates configuration, Inspector scans compute — none classifies data content.

evidence: det.txt

GuardDuty finding: compromised role.
Need: trace every API call and
network flow from that role,
visualized over time.
scenarios.hint: Which service builds the investigation graph from the logs you already have?
scenarios.situation: A compromised role needs full tracing of its API calls and network flows, visualized over time.
scenarios.title: Tracing the compromised role
scenarios.why: Detective ingests CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and GuardDuty findings into an interactive investigation graph — built for exactly this 'what did the compromised entity touch' analysis. Manual review is slow; CloudTrail alone lacks the graph; Config tracks configuration, not activity.

choices: AWS Shield Advanced with automatic application-layer DDoS mitigation
evidence: ddos.txt

Attack: 2M rps HTTP flood,
rotating IPs, targeting login.
Shield Standard absorbing L3/L4.
scenarios.hint: L3/L4 is absorbed — what handles the Layer 7 flood with AWS support?
scenarios.situation: A 2M rps HTTP flood from rotating IPs targets login; Shield Standard already absorbs the network layer.
scenarios.title: Two million requests per second
scenarios.why: Shield Advanced adds application-layer DDoS protection with automatic mitigation, the Shield Response Team (SRT), and cost protection. WAF rate-based rules help but lack SRT and automatic L7 mitigation; security groups can't filter rotating floods at this scale; Network Firewall is VPC-level.

choices: CloudTrail with log file validation to an S3 bucket with Object Lock
evidence: forensic.txt

Requirement: tamper-evident API
history, 2-year retention, usable
in legal proceedings.
scenarios.hint: Which combination gives integrity validation plus WORM retention?
scenarios.prompt: Which logging design is forensically sound?
scenarios.situation: API history must be tamper-evident, retained 2 years, and defensible in legal proceedings.
scenarios.title: Evidence-grade logging
scenarios.why: CloudTrail with log file validation (digest files proving integrity) delivered to an S3 bucket with Object Lock (WORM) gives tamper-evident, immutable, long-retention API history. Short CloudWatch retention, 90-day console history, and app logs don't meet the bar.

choices: VPC Flow Logs with default format
VPC Flow Logs with custom format including pkt-srcaddr/pkt-dstaddr
evidence: nat2.txt

Traffic through NAT gateway.
Need: identify which private instance
opened each connection.
scenarios.hint: Behind NAT, the source IP is the NAT's — which fields reveal the original?
scenarios.situation: Traffic flows through a NAT gateway; investigators must identify which private instance opened each connection.
scenarios.title: Who's behind the NAT?
scenarios.why: Custom-format VPC Flow Logs with pkt-srcaddr/pkt-dstaddr fields capture the original packet addresses before NAT translation — the only way to attribute connections behind NAT. Default format lacks these fields; security groups don't log; DNS logs show queries, not connections.

evidence: s3audit.txt

Requirement: log every GET/PUT
on the financial-records bucket:
who, when, which object.
scenarios.hint: Management events won't show object reads — which event type does?
scenarios.situation: Every GET/PUT on a financial-records bucket must be logged with identity, time, and object.
scenarios.title: Who read the financial records?
scenarios.why: CloudTrail data events log object-level S3 API calls (GetObject, PutObject) with identity and object details. Management events cover bucket-level operations only; S3 access logs are an older alternative but CloudTrail data events are the modern audit answer; Flow Logs and metrics don't identify S3 access.

choices: A dedicated audit/log-archive account with no workload access
Logs in the same bucket as the data
evidence: org.txt

12 accounts. Requirement: security
team reads all logs; workload teams
cannot modify or delete them.
scenarios.hint: Where should logs live so workload teams can't touch them?
scenarios.situation: Twelve accounts; the security team must read all logs while workload teams cannot modify or delete them.
scenarios.title: Logs nobody can delete
scenarios.why: A dedicated log-archive account (per AWS landing-zone guidance) centralizes logs where workload teams have no write access — enforcing separation of duties. In-account logs let workload teams tamper; co-locating with data risks both; no centralization blocks investigation.

choices: Athena querying CloudTrail logs in S3
evidence: query.txt

Question: which principals called
 iam:CreateUser in the last 90 days,
across all regions?
scenarios.hint: 90 days of API history across regions, in S3 — which serverless SQL queries it?
scenarios.situation: The team must find which principals called iam:CreateUser in the last 90 days across all regions.
scenarios.title: Ninety days of API calls
scenarios.why: CloudTrail logs in S3 queried with Athena give serverless SQL over months of history across regions. The console's event history is 90 days but not cross-region queryable at scale; Logs Insights queries CloudWatch Logs, not the S3 archive; Config tracks resource state, not API calls.

evidence: top.txt

Need: top talkers by IP,
heaviest S3 prefixes, top
DynamoDB keys — continuously.
scenarios.hint: Which CloudWatch feature ranks top contributors from logs?
scenarios.prompt: What identifies the top contributors continuously?
scenarios.situation: The team needs continuous ranking of top talkers by IP, heaviest S3 prefixes, and hottest DynamoDB keys.
scenarios.title: Finding the top talkers
scenarios.why: CloudWatch Contributor Insights analyzes log data (VPC Flow Logs, etc.) to rank top-N contributors continuously with rules. Default metrics don't rank; raw Flow Logs need analysis; X-Ray traces requests, not top-talker aggregation.

choices: Private subnets + Systems Manager Session Manager, no public IPs
evidence: infra.txt

Requirement: no instance reachable
from the internet; admin access
audited; no key management.
scenarios.hint: Which access method needs no bastion, no public IP, and logs to CloudTrail?
scenarios.situation: No instance may be internet-reachable; admin access must be audited with no SSH key management.
scenarios.title: No SSH from the internet, ever
scenarios.why: Private subnets with Session Manager give audited shell access with no public IPs, no bastions, and no SSH keys — every session logged. Public subnets and open bastions violate the requirement; VPN without MFA is weak.

choices: AWS Network Firewall with Suricata-compatible rules
evidence: egress.txt
scenarios.hint: Which managed service does stateful Layer 3-7 inspection with IPS rules?
scenarios.situation: All VPC egress must be inspected and filtered with IPS signatures and C2 domain blocking.
scenarios.title: Inspecting everything leaving
scenarios.why: AWS Network Firewall provides managed stateful inspection with Suricata-compatible IPS rules and domain filtering for VPC traffic. Security groups/NACLs filter but don't do IPS; WAF protects ALB/CloudFront-facing apps, not VPC egress.

choices: Security groups with least-privilege ingress + AWS Config rule to detect drift
One security group for all tiers
evidence: sg2.txt

Tiers: web, app, db.
Requirement: only web gets internet
traffic; db only from app tier.
scenarios.hint: Which pattern gives tier isolation with continuous verification?
scenarios.situation: Web, app, and DB tiers need strict isolation: internet only to web, DB only from app.
scenarios.title: Three tiers, three perimeters
scenarios.why: Least-privilege security groups per tier (web←internet, app←web, db←app) enforce the isolation, with a Config rule catching drift. Open ingress or one shared group destroys the tiering; disabling groups removes the control.

choices: TLS everywhere with ACM-managed certificates and TLS policies
Terminating TLS at the client only
evidence: tls.txt

Requirement: encrypt all traffic
in transit, managed rotation,
no expired-cert outages.
scenarios.hint: Which ACM feature eliminates expired-cert outages?
scenarios.situation: All traffic must be encrypted in transit with managed rotation and no expired-certificate outages.
scenarios.title: TLS without the expiry panic
scenarios.why: ACM-managed certificates with automatic renewal on AWS-integrated services (ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway) plus enforced TLS policies give encryption in transit without expiry outages. Plain HTTP fails the requirement; self-signed certs create rotation pain.

evidence: ssrf.txt

App had SSRF vulnerability.
Attacker read instance credentials
via the metadata service.
scenarios.hint: Which IMDS version requires a PUT token, defeating simple SSRF reads?
scenarios.prompt: What prevents credential theft via SSRF?
scenarios.situation: An SSRF vulnerability let an attacker read instance credentials from the metadata service.
scenarios.title: The SSRF that stole credentials
scenarios.why: IMDSv2 requires a session token obtained via PUT request, which simple SSRF GET attacks can't perform — enforcing it instance-wide mitigates credential theft. IMDSv1's plain GETs are the vulnerability; disabling metadata breaks legitimate uses; user-data credentials are worse.

choices: Dedicated inspection VPC with Transit Gateway + Network Firewall
evidence: central.txt

20 VPCs. Requirement: central
inspection of all inter-VPC and
egress traffic.
scenarios.hint: Which architecture centralizes inspection without N-squared peering?
scenarios.situation: Twenty VPCs need centralized inspection of inter-VPC and egress traffic.
scenarios.title: Inspecting twenty VPCs centrally
scenarios.why: A dedicated inspection VPC with Transit Gateway routing all traffic through Network Firewall centralizes inspection scalably. One VPC destroys isolation; full peering mesh is unmanageable; no inspection fails the requirement.

choices: An ABAC policy: allow actions where aws:PrincipalTag/team == resource tag team
No policy; use the root user
evidence: abac.txt

500 engineers, 60 projects.
Need: engineers manage only
resources tagged with their team.
scenarios.hint: Which condition compares principal tags to resource tags?
scenarios.situation: 500 engineers across 60 projects; each engineer should manage only resources tagged with their team.
scenarios.title: Authorization by tag
scenarios.why: ABAC with conditions comparing aws:PrincipalTag/team to the resource's team tag scales to any number of teams with one policy. Per-team policies explode; AdministratorAccess violates least privilege; root is never the answer.

choices: Cross-account IAM roles with external ID
evidence: xacct.txt

Vendor needs read access to
specific S3 prefixes in your account.
Requirement: no long-term keys,
protected against confused deputy.
scenarios.hint: Which two features combine for safe third-party access?
scenarios.prompt: What grants the vendor access safely?
scenarios.situation: A vendor needs read access to specific S3 prefixes; no long-term keys allowed, confused-deputy protection required.
scenarios.title: The vendor needs access
scenarios.why: Cross-account IAM roles give temporary credentials scoped to the prefixes, and the external ID condition prevents the confused-deputy attack where the vendor could be tricked into acting on another customer's resources. Shared keys violate the no-long-term-keys rule.

choices: IAM Identity Center with MFA + permission sets, short-term credentials
evidence: workforce.txt

200 employees, 15 accounts.
Need: SSO, MFA enforced,
least privilege, no static keys.
scenarios.hint: Which service is built for workforce SSO across accounts?
scenarios.situation: 200 employees across 15 accounts need SSO with enforced MFA, least privilege, and no static keys.
scenarios.title: Workforce identity at scale
scenarios.why: IAM Identity Center provides SSO across accounts with MFA enforcement and permission sets issuing short-term credentials. Static keys, shared passwords, and embedded API keys all fail the requirements.

choices: IAM Roles Anywhere for on-prem workloads with X.509 certificates
Opening the VPC to the internet
evidence: onprem.txt

On-prem servers need AWS API
access. No static keys allowed.
Workloads have X.509 certs.
scenarios.hint: Which service exchanges X.509 certificates for temporary AWS credentials?
scenarios.prompt: What gives on-prem servers temporary credentials?
scenarios.situation: On-premises servers with X.509 certificates need AWS API access without static keys.
scenarios.title: Credentials for the data center
scenarios.why: IAM Roles Anywhere lets on-premises workloads exchange X.509 certificates for temporary AWS credentials via a trust anchor — extending IAM roles beyond AWS. Static keys violate the policy; trust alone isn't authentication.

choices: A policy with explicit Deny on sensitive actions + permission boundaries on roles
evidence: guard.txt

Requirement: even admins cannot
delete CloudTrail logs or the
log-archive bucket.
scenarios.hint: Which two mechanisms combine to make a denial unbypassable?
scenarios.prompt: What makes the protection hold against admins?
scenarios.situation: Even administrators must be unable to delete CloudTrail logs or the log-archive bucket.
scenarios.title: Deny, even for admins
scenarios.why: An explicit Deny in an SCP (Organizations) or permissions boundary overrides any Allow — even for admins — making the log protection hold. Allow-only policies can't restrain admins; trust isn't a control; disabling CloudTrail is the opposite of the goal.

evidence: unused.txt

3 years of accumulated policies.
Need: find unused permissions and
generate least-privilege policies.
scenarios.hint: Which service analyzes CloudTrail to show what was actually used?
scenarios.situation: Three years of accumulated IAM policies need trimming to least privilege.
scenarios.title: Trimming three years of policies
scenarios.why: IAM Access Analyzer analyzes CloudTrail activity to identify unused permissions and can generate least-privilege policies from actual usage. Manual reviews don't scale across years of accumulation; guessing is dangerous; Trusted Advisor checks basics, not usage-based refinement.

choices: SSE-KMS with customer managed keys + key policies
Client-side encryption with keys on a sticky note
evidence: cmk.txt

Regulated data. Need: control key
access per team, audit every use,
rotate annually, revoke instantly.
scenarios.hint: Which option gives you key policies, rotation, and per-use CloudTrail logging?
scenarios.prompt: Which encryption design meets the requirements?
scenarios.situation: Regulated data needs per-team key access control, audited use, annual rotation, and instant revocation.
scenarios.title: Keys with an audit trail
scenarios.why: SSE-KMS with customer managed keys provides key policies (per-team control), automatic rotation, CloudTrail logging of every use, and instant revocation via policy. SSE-S3 offers no key control or audit; client-side sticky-note keys are a breach.

choices: Separate KMS keys per data classification with key policies
evidence: sep.txt

Data: public, internal, confidential,
restricted. Requirement: separation
of duties for key admins.
scenarios.hint: How do you give different admins control over different data classes?
scenarios.situation: Four data classifications need separation of duties among key administrators.
scenarios.title: One key per kingdom
scenarios.why: Separate customer managed keys per classification with distinct key policies let different admins control different data classes. One key can't separate duties; AWS-managed keys offer no key policies; config-file keys are insecure.

choices: S3 Object Lock (Compliance mode) + MFA Delete on versioned buckets
evidence: ransom.txt

Threat: ransomware encrypting S3
objects and deleting versions.
Need: immutable, recoverable.
scenarios.hint: What makes objects undeletable even by compromised admin credentials?
scenarios.prompt: What protects the backups from ransomware?
scenarios.situation: Ransomware threatens to encrypt S3 objects and delete versions; backups must be immutable and recoverable.
scenarios.title: Backups ransomware can't touch
scenarios.why: Object Lock Compliance mode makes objects immutable even to admins/root until retention expires, and MFA Delete adds protection on versioned buckets — ransomware with stolen credentials still can't destroy the data. Versioning alone allows version deletion; expiration deletes; manual backups are unreliable.

choices: TLS 1.2+ enforced via policies (ALB/CloudFront security policies, S3 bucket policies)
evidence: transit.txt

Requirement: encrypt all data in
transit, minimum TLS 1.2,
verified continuously.
scenarios.hint: Which mechanisms enforce the TLS version at each integration point?
scenarios.situation: All data in transit must use TLS 1.2 or higher, verified continuously.
scenarios.title: TLS 1.2 or nothing
scenarios.why: Enforcing TLS 1.2+ via ALB/CloudFront security policies and S3 bucket policies (aws:SecureTransport + TLS version conditions) with Config rules verifying continuously meets the requirement at every layer. TLS 1.0 and HTTP fail it; unvalidated self-signed certs break trust.

choices: Tokenization/vaulting: store tokens, keep real PANs in a hardened vault (or outsource to a compliant processor)
evidence: pci.txt
scenarios.hint: What removes the sensitive value from your systems entirely?
scenarios.situation: An app handles card numbers; operators must never see PANs and PCI scope must be minimal.
scenarios.title: Never seeing the card number
scenarios.why: Tokenization replaces PANs with tokens in your systems (or outsources to a compliant processor), removing card data from scope — operators literally cannot see what isn't there. Storing tokens-as-PANs, encryption alone, and hashing all keep PAN-derived data in your environment.

choices: Customer managed keys with automatic rotation enabled
evidence: rot2.txt

Policy: rotate encryption keys
annually, automatically,
with audit trail.
scenarios.hint: Which KMS feature rotates without application changes?
scenarios.situation: Encryption keys must rotate annually, automatically, with an audit trail.
scenarios.title: Rotation on autopilot
scenarios.why: Customer managed keys with automatic rotation rotate annually in KMS with full CloudTrail audit and no application changes (the key ID stays the same). AWS-managed keys rotate on AWS's schedule, not yours; manual rotation is error-prone; no rotation violates policy.

choices: Quarantine with security groups, capture memory/disk forensics, then terminate
evidence: ec2ir.txt

EC2 confirmed compromised.
Need: stop spread, preserve
evidence, eradicate.
scenarios.hint: Contain, collect evidence, then eradicate — which option does all three?
scenarios.situation: An EC2 instance is confirmed compromised; the team must stop spread, preserve evidence, and eradicate.
scenarios.title: The compromised instance
scenarios.why: Security-group quarantine stops lateral movement, forensic capture (EBS snapshots, memory) preserves evidence, then termination eradicates — the standard sequence. Immediate termination destroys evidence; watching lets it spread; rebooting changes evidence state.

choices: Immediate key deactivation/rotation, CloudTrail review, scope check via Access Analyzer
evidence: keyir.txt

IAM user key found in a public
repo. Unknown if exploited.
scenarios.hint: Assume breach: what makes the key useless and tells you if it was used?
scenarios.situation: An IAM access key is found in a public repo; exploitation is unknown.
scenarios.title: Assume the key is burned
scenarios.why: Deactivate/rotate the key immediately (making it useless), review CloudTrail for misuse, and check the blast radius via Access Analyzer. Waiting risks exploitation; password changes don't affect access keys.

choices: S3 Block Public Access + bucket policy review + CloudTrail data-event review
Making the bucket private next quarter
evidence: s3ir.txt

Alert: sensitive bucket became
public. Unknown exposure window.
scenarios.hint: Stop the bleeding, assess the exposure, then harden — which option does that?
scenarios.situation: A sensitive bucket became public with an unknown exposure window.
scenarios.title: The bucket went public
scenarios.why: Block Public Access stops the bleeding immediately, policy review finds the cause, and CloudTrail data-event review determines what was accessed during the window. Deletion destroys evidence; delay extends exposure.

choices: A pre-built forensic account + automated evidence collection runbooks
Ad-hoc investigation in the production account
evidence: prep.txt

Requirement: be ready to investigate
the next incident in minutes,
not days.
scenarios.hint: What do mature teams build before the incident?
scenarios.situation: The team must be able to investigate the next incident in minutes, not days.
scenarios.title: Ready before it happens
scenarios.why: A pre-built forensic account with automated evidence-collection runbooks (isolate, snapshot, capture logs) makes investigation minutes-fast. Ad-hoc production investigation risks evidence and production; no preparation guarantees days-long response.

choices: Containment, eradication, recovery, then blameless postmortem with tracked actions
evidence: lifecycle.txt

Incident contained.
Leadership asks: what now?
scenarios.hint: Which lifecycle turns the incident into lasting improvement?
scenarios.situation: An incident is contained; leadership asks what comes next.
scenarios.title: After containment
scenarios.why: The full lifecycle — eradication, recovery, then a blameless postmortem with tracked action items — converts the incident into systemic improvement. Starting over wastes the learning; blame suppresses honesty; skipping the postmortem guarantees repeats.

choices: SSM Incident Manager with runbooks, paging, and timelines
evidence: coord2.txt

SEV-1: 5 teams, 3 time zones.
Need: clear roles, decision log,
runbook execution.
scenarios.hint: Which service orchestrates the human side of incidents?
scenarios.situation: A SEV-1 spans 5 teams and 3 time zones; roles, decision logs, and runbook execution must be clear.
scenarios.title: Coordinating across time zones
scenarios.why: SSM Incident Manager provides response plans, paging, runbook execution, and decision timelines for multi-team incidents. Email threads lose decisions; shared docs don't page; verbal updates leave no record.

Describe a time you responded to a security incident.
Tell me about a time you had to balance security with usability or speed.
Describe a time you implemented a security control across many accounts or teams.
Tell me about a time you had to explain a security risk to non-technical leadership.
Describe a time you automated a security process.
Tell me about a time you dealt with a compliance requirement.
Describe a time you learned a new attack technique or defense and applied it.
